# Inverse-convex targets and retained-mass repairs fail for every uniform coupling

This is an exact consequence of the stronger target-depth obstruction
in `candidate 3afcec5ae41ce7af`, with a new explicit
minorant budget. It tests the actual target in
`candidate ddedecc7f627090b`, allowing arbitrary dependence
between its two uniform endpoint marginals. It does not test arbitrary
nonuniform source selections or every possible halfspace-dominated
target measure.

## 1. Actual convex fibers in the hard volume range

In two continuous dimensions put

`T=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)}`,
`A=conv{(0,0),(4/5,0),(0,8/25)}`,

`epsilon=2^(-20)`, `s=3/128+epsilon`,
`K_-=(2-s)A`, `K_+=sA`.

Let C be the convex hull of these bodies at the three integer levels
-1, 0, 1, with middle body T. These are its exact integer fibers:
the endpoints are extreme, and `(K_-+K_+)/2=A subset T` prevents
enlargement of the middle fiber. Thus C is a full-dimensional convex
body in `R x R^2` with exactly three positive-area integer fibers.

Write `c=|T|=1/2`, `a=|K_-|`, `b=|K_+|`, `M=a+b+c`, and

`e=(32/125)s^2=604028929/4294967296000`,
`delta=(128/125)epsilon=1/1024000`.

The exact area relations are

`a/c=1+e-delta`, `b/c=e`, `M/c=2+2e-delta`.

All three fiber areas are strictly below M/2, a>b, and zero is the
unique weighted median integer index. These strict rational inequalities
are verified in the original certificate. Hence the example lies in
the requested hard range; a heavy fiber or an alternative median fiber
does not bypass it.

For an arbitrary coupling pi of uniform X in K_- and uniform Y in K_+,
define

`Z=(X+Y)/2`, `eta_pi=1_T dx+b Law_pi(Z)`.

This includes the product coupling in the original construction and
every possible change of dependence with the same uniform marginals.
Its exact mass is

\[
 W=c+b=\frac M2+\frac1{4096000}>\frac M2.                 \tag{1}
\]

The original closed ambient halfspace domination `eta_pi(H)<=mu(H)`
continues to hold for every such coupling, because a midpoint in H
has at least one endpoint in H and b<=a. No repeated transport or
density-preserving iteration is used.

## 2. Three cap bounds uniform over all couplings

Put

`a0=1/3-e/16`, `b0=1/3-41e/125`,
`alpha=1-s/2`, `beta=s/2`,
`u=5a0/4`, `v=5(a0+b0)/4`.

The three fixed closed halfplanes

`H1={x>=a0}`, `H2={y>=b0}`, `H3={x+y<=a0+b0}`

cover the whole continuous plane. The original note proves, without
any regularity assumption on pi, that

\[
 \eta_\pi(H_i)\le c U_i,
\]

where

\[
 \begin{split}
 U_1&=(1-a_0)^2+e((1-u)/\alpha)^2,\\
 U_2&=(1-b_0)^2,\\
 U_3&=(a_0+b_0)^2+
       e\left[1-\frac{((\alpha-v)/\alpha)^2}{3/5}\right].
 \end{split}                                                \tag{2}
\]

For completeness, write X=(2-s)U and Y=sV, where both U,V are uniform
on A. The events for H1 force
`U_x/(4/5)>=(u-beta)/alpha`, whose marginal tail is
`((1-u)/alpha)^2`; H2 catches no endpoint midpoint because its threshold
exceeds the maximum y-coordinate of A. The strict event
`(U_x+U_y)/(4/5)>v/alpha` forces Z outside the closed H3; its marginal
probability is `((alpha-v)/alpha)^2/(3/5)`. These implications give
(2) even when Z has mass on a cap boundary. The middle-fiber terms
are the three elementary similar-triangle areas of T.

With `gamma_2=4/9`, the rational comparisons in the supplied verifier
give, for every i,

\[
 \frac{\gamma_2 M}{2c}-U_i>\frac6{10^7}.
\]

Since c=1/2, this is the convenient uniform absolute bound

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \eta_\pi(H_i)<\frac{\gamma_2 M}{2}-\frac3{10^7}
 \qquad(i=1,2,3),
 \quad}                                                     \tag{3}
\]

for every coupling pi. Every point of the plane belongs to one of
these caps. Therefore the maximum unnormalized halfspace depth of
eta_pi is strictly below the right side of (3).

## 3. Failure of the weaker inverse-power convexity requirement

The proved density theorem in
`candidate f9c635ce5abe9f17` says that a
bounded compactly supported two-dimensional density f with
`f^(-1/3)` convex, extended by infinity where f=0, has a point of
unnormalized depth at least `gamma_2 integral f`. It applies to exactly
the weaker density class proposed for the median target.

No eta_pi in Section 1 can be such a density. Otherwise its mass W
would give a depth point of value at least gamma_2 W, which by (1)
is greater than gamma_2 M/2, contradicting (3). Multiplying a density
by its normalization constant does not change convexity of its
negative one-third power, so normalizing eta_pi to probability does
not repair the obstruction.

There is no unbounded-density loophole in this claim. More generally,
let f be integrable with positive full-dimensional convex support in
R^p and let `q=f^(-1/(p+1))` be extended-real convex. Choose an interior
ball of radius r on which q<=C<infinity. If at another domain point
q(x)=epsilon lies in `(0,C]`, set `lambda=epsilon/C`. Convexity bounds
q by `2epsilon` on the ball obtained by interpolating x with this fixed
ball at weight lambda. Consequently, writing m=integral f,

`m >= omega_p r^p lambda^p/(2epsilon)^(p+1)
    = omega_p r^p/[2^(p+1) C^p epsilon]`.

Thus q is uniformly bounded below by a positive constant wherever it
is at most C, and f is bounded everywhere. If q(x)=0, the same argument
with arbitrary lambda>0 makes the displayed mass lower bound diverge
as lambda decreases to zero, which is impossible. Taking the lower
semicontinuous closure of q changes it only on the boundary of its
convex domain, a Lebesgue-null set, and the positive lower bound is
preserved. This supplies a bounded upper-semicontinuous representative
of f. In the present target its support is T, so the compact-support
density theorem applies. Hence **no integrable density representative
of any eta_pi can have convex inverse one-third power**, even if no
boundedness was required initially.

Likewise, no absolutely continuous eta_pi can have a **convex** radial
Ball body, preserving through-point cap fractions, when radialized at
one of its deepest points. Here is the precise implication, rather
than an assumption that an arbitrary radial origin is a centroid.
The uniform background on T supplies a positive lower density on every
interior ball. Cap masses for an absolutely continuous compactly
supported measure are jointly continuous in point and normal. Its
deepest point is attained in int T, and the elementary slab-improvement
argument from the cited note supplies a finite positively balanced
family of active normals. If a convex radial body at that point
preserved those cap fractions, they would cover the whole plane with
each cap having the target's maximum-depth fraction. Applying ordinary
Grünbaum at the radial body's actual centroid would give depth at
least gamma_2 W, again contradicting (3).

This argument does not require the coupling density to be bounded:
absolute continuity gives cap continuity, and the fixed uniform
background gives the uniform positive slab increase for active normals.
If a chosen coupling makes eta_pi singular, it is already outside the
stated density class; (3) itself still applies to it.

## 4. Quantitative obstruction to a retained-mass minorant

Let xi be any finite nonzero measure with `xi<=eta_pi`, and suppose
xi belongs to any class having the following ordinary continuous
centerpoint property in the plane:

`some point has xi-halfspace depth at least gamma_2 xi(R^2)`.

This includes full-dimensional log-concave measures, the bounded compact
inverse-cube-convex density class above, and lower-dimensional
log-concave measures: on a line the median has depth at least one half,
and a point mass has depth one, both at least gamma_2.

Let R=xi(R^2) and choose such a depth point. One of H1,H2,H3 contains
it, so (3) and domination give

`gamma_2 R<=xi(H_i)<=eta_pi(H_i)<gamma_2 M/2-3/10^7`.

Consequently

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 R<\frac M2-\frac{27}{40000000}.
 \quad}                                                     \tag{4}
\]

Combining this with (1), every such minorant must discard mass strictly
more than

\[
 W-R>
 \frac1{4096000}+\frac{27}{40000000}.                       \tag{5}
\]

In particular a log-concave or inverse-convex minorant cannot retain
the mass M/2 needed for the original factor-two halfspace domination
after normalization. This rules out the repair even though the initial
target has strictly positive domination slack W-M/2.

## Scope

The obstruction is uniform over all couplings of the two original
uniform endpoint laws, including singular couplings. It closes the
precise target construction, its inverse-power-density relaxation,
convex radialization at a deepest point, and its dominated minorant
repair at the required retained mass. It does not exclude selecting
a nonuniform submeasure of the larger endpoint, changing the central
singleton allocation, or another target that is not a minorant of one
of these eta_pi. It does not refute OC or the already proved median
fiber domination by an arbitrary probability law.
